stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The manager was ADAMANT about the new rule.
explanationCorrect: Adamant means refusing to change one's mind — firm, unyielding.

explanationsWrong.B: Confused means unsure, the opposite of adamant.

stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: Her CANDID reply surprised everyone.
explanationCorrect: Candid means honest and direct — frank.

explanationsWrong.A: A candid reply may be blunt, but candid doesn't mean rude.
explanationsWrong.B: Delayed relates to time, not honesty.

stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The villagers were HOSTILE to the strangers.
explanationCorrect: Hostile means unfriendly or aggressive; its opposite is friendly.

explanationsWrong.A: Unfriendly is a synonym, not an antonym.
explanationsWrong.B: Indifferent means not caring — not the opposite of hostile.
explanationsWrong.D: Suspicious is closer to hostile than opposite.

stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: She gave a LUCID explanation of the problem.
explanationCorrect: Lucid means clear and easy to understand; the opposite is confusing (obscure).

explanationsWrong.A: Clear is a synonym of lucid.
explanationsWrong.C: Brief is about length, not clarity.
explanationsWrong.D: Detailed is about amount of information.

stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Neither the teacher nor the students ______ present.
explanationCorrect: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Students' is plural, so 'were'.

explanationsWrong.B: 'Was' would agree with 'teacher', but the nearer subject is 'students'.

stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Each of the boys ______ a new book.
explanationCorrect: 'Each' is singular, so the verb is singular: 'has'.

explanationsWrong.A: 'Have' agrees with 'boys', but the subject is 'each'.
explanationsWrong.B: Plural verb — 'each' needs a singular verb.
explanationsWrong.C: Plural verb and the wrong tense.

stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: By this time next year, she ______ her degree.
explanationCorrect: An action finished before a point in the future takes the future perfect: will have completed.

explanationsWrong.A: Simple present doesn't express completion by a future time.
explanationsWrong.B: Simple future doesn't show the action finished before that time.
explanationsWrong.D: Present perfect refers to the past up to now.

stem: Choose the correct question tag: You aren't coming with us, ______?
explanationCorrect: A negative statement takes a positive tag with the same auxiliary: 'are you?'

explanationsWrong.A: A negative statement needs a positive tag.

stem: Choose the correct question tag: Let's go to the library, ______?
explanationCorrect: Sentences beginning with 'Let's' take the tag 'shall we?'

explanationsWrong.B: 'Will we' isn't the standard tag for 'Let's'.
explanationsWrong.D: 'Let's' includes the speaker, so the tag uses 'we'.

stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Amaka is very good ______ mathematics.
explanationCorrect: The standard preposition after 'good' for skill is 'at': good at mathematics.

explanationsWrong.A: 'Good in' is common in speech but not standard.
explanationsWrong.B: 'Good with' is used for people or tools (good with children).

stem: Choose the option that best explains the expression in capitals: After years of quarrelling, the two families decided to BURY THE HATCHET.
explanationCorrect: 'Bury the hatchet' means to end a quarrel and make peace.

explanationsWrong.A: That's the literal meaning, not the idiomatic one.
explanationsWrong.B: Going to court would continue the quarrel.
explanationsWrong.D: The idiom has nothing to do with farming.

stem: Choose the option that best explains the expression in capitals: Don't invite Musa; he is such A WET BLANKET.

options.B: someone who spoils other people's fun

explanationCorrect: A wet blanket is a person who dampens other people's enjoyment.

explanationsWrong.A: That's a literal reading of the words.

stem: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: Tunde took the rumour with a pinch of salt.

options.A: He did not fully believe it.

explanationCorrect: To take something with a pinch of salt means to doubt it or not believe it entirely.

explanationsWrong.B: It means the opposite — doubting, not believing.

stem: Choose the correctly spelt word.
explanationCorrect: 'Accommodation' has double c and double m.

stem: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one in 'fool'.
explanationCorrect: 'Fool' and 'rule' both have the long vowel /uː/.

stem: Choose the word that begins with the same consonant sound as 'phone'.
explanationCorrect: 'Ph' in 'phone' is pronounced /f/, the same as the f in 'fish'.

stem: Choose the word that rhymes with 'said'.
explanationCorrect: 'Said' is pronounced /sed/, rhyming with 'bed'.

stem: Choose the option with the correct stress (capitals show the stressed syllable): photograph
explanationCorrect: 'Photograph' is stressed on the first syllable: PHO-to-graph. (Compare pho-TO-gra-pher.)

explanationsWrong.C: Only one syllable carries primary stress.

stem: In 'Please keep a RECORD of the meeting', the word 'record' is a noun. Which syllable is stressed?
explanationCorrect: Many two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable as nouns (REcord) and the second as verbs (reCORD).

explanationsWrong.A: Second-syllable stress is for the verb 'to record'.
explanationsWrong.B: English words have one primary stress.
explanationsWrong.D: Every English word of two syllables has one stressed syllable.

stem: In the sentence 'JOHN bought the car', the emphatic stress is on 'John'. Which question does it answer?
explanationCorrect: Stressing 'John' highlights who did the action.
